Bravo! You\'ve finished all cards in the selected decks.
New cards will show up here when it\'s time to study.
Cards come from the first deck below that has one to review, then the next one. A deck includes its subdecks. Cards with sound in the question are skipped.
Tick decks in the list below to review them.
Either AnkiDroid is not installed, or its API is disabled. Enable it in AnkiDroid: Settings › Advanced › Enable AnkiDroid API.
Micro Review for AnkiDroid needs access to your AnkiDroid cards to show them.

AnkiDroid didn\'t give its decks: it may be updating, or its collection may be closed. Open AnkiDroid, then retry. If you just enabled its API, close AnkiDroid from the recent apps and open it again first.
Notifications are disabled: the monitor\'s notification and its Snooze buttons won\'t show. Enable them in the app\'s system settings.
Permission to read AnkiDroid cards was not granted.
Opens a new issue on GitHub, with your phone model, Android version and app versions already filled in. You can check and edit everything before sending it.
No browser found to open GitHub.
The license of this app and of the libraries it uses.
Background activity is restricted for this app, so the cards may stop coming. Set its battery usage to Optimized or Unrestricted.
Cards while you use your phone
A card pops up every so often while the screen is on and unlocked. Never shown on the lock screen.
Kept running so cards can come while you use your phone and chosen apps can be gated. Its buttons snooze the cards.
Cards come while you use your phone.
Your chosen apps ask for cards first.
Cards come while you use your phone, and your chosen apps ask for cards first.
Quiet hours: no cards for now.
Do Not Disturb is on: no cards for now.
In a call: no cards for now.
Your PC is in use: everything is paused.
Bluetooth device connected: everything is paused.
Next card in %1$d min of use.

If Android says a setting is restricted for this app: open the app\'s info page (long-press its icon, then App info), tap the three dots, then \"Allow restricted settings\", and come back.
Lets the app see which app is in front, to time the cards per app and to gate the apps you chose. Nothing leaves your phone.
Lets the gate and full-screen cards open over the app in front.
For the monitor\'s notification, its Snooze buttons, and a card when it can\'t take the screen.
No cards for a while. Also on the monitor\'s notification and on each card.
Off: a snooze stops the cards, but gated apps still ask for theirs.
Cards while you use your phone

A card pops up every so often, only while the screen is on and unlocked, never on the lock screen. Answer it and you\'re done, or keep going. A card you don\'t touch is withdrawn, so its time doesn\'t count.
None. For example a card every 5 minutes on your biggest time wasters, or never on your maps app.
Show the note\'s fields under the answer
On the full-screen card: every field of the note the card didn\'t show, such as the meaning or the reading, so a definition left off the card\'s back is still there.
Pass records Good and Fail records Again. Hard and Easy are never offered, anywhere in the app.
Ask for cards before chosen apps
Opening one of them first asks for a few cards. Pass or Fail, each answer counts. No grace period: close the app and open it again, and it asks again. Nothing due means no gate.
While a Bluetooth device is connected
Everything pauses: no cards, and the gate is open. For example in the car or with headphones at work.
Without the \"Nearby devices\" permission, only Bluetooth audio (car, headphones, speakers) is detected, not watches or keyboards.
No cards while Do Not Disturb or another mode silences notifications.
No cards while you are in a call.
None. For example no cards from 22:00 to 07:00.
Pause while my PC is in use
With Micro Review Desktop, the Anki add-on, on your PC: cards and the gate pause for 5 minutes after you last use its mouse or keyboard.
In Anki on your PC: Tools › Micro Review Desktop. Type the pairing code shown there.
Pause while my PC is in use
No cards, the gate is open, for 5 minutes after you last use your PC\'s mouse or keyboard. Your PC tells the phone through ntfy.sh, a free relay: only a number of seconds is sent.
Answers wait to be synced: as your next card screen closes, or now. Asked last: %1$s.

Nothing waiting. Asked AnkiDroid last: %1$s. AnkiDroid only syncs with its screen up for a moment, so it\'s only asked as a card screen closes, hidden behind it. Cards your PC reviewed are skipped until then.
Copied: paste it where you report the problem.
Turn on nudges or the app gate in Settings.
Four looks from the glossy years, shuffled or locked.
Shuffling: a new theme each time the app or a card opens, from the ticked ones. Tap a theme to tick or untick it. Lock to keep the one showing.
Locked on %1$s. Tap a theme to switch to it, or unlock to shuffle again.
Cards, the gate, pauses and the look
What the monitor sees and did, to tell why a card or the gate didn\'t come.

Lie on your stomach, hands under your shoulders. Push your chest up while your hips stay on the floor and your back stays relaxed, then lower. Go a little higher each time, as far as is comfortable. The main tool: morning, evening, and whenever the leg acts up.
On hands and knees, back flat. Reach one arm forward and the opposite leg back, level with your body, without letting your back sag or twist. Hold, come back, switch.
On your side, elbow under your shoulder, knees bent. Lift your hips until you\'re straight from knees to head. Hold, lower.
On your back, one knee bent, the other leg straight, hands under the small of your back. Lift your head and shoulders a little, as one block: no curling of the neck or the lower back. Hold, lower.
On your back, knees bent, feet flat. Squeeze your glutes and lift your hips until you\'re straight from shoulders to knees, without arching. Hold, lower slowly.

Stand with soft knees. Push your hips back as if closing a car door behind you, chest forward, back straight. Come up by squeezing your glutes. This is how you bend: for socks, the floor, the dishwasher.
Standing tall or lying on your back: glide your head straight back, making a double chin, eyes level, until the back of your neck lengthens. Hold, relax. Against a head that drifts forward.
Arms by your sides, or elbows bent at your sides. Draw your shoulder blades back and down, toward your back pockets, without shrugging or arching. Hold, relax.
Forearm on a door frame, elbow at shoulder height. Step through gently until the front of your chest stretches. Ribs down, no arching.
Head, upper back and hips against a wall, feet a step out. Arms in a W against the wall: slide them up to a Y and back down, only as far as they stay on the wall.

Kneel on one knee on a cushion, the other foot in front. Tuck your tailbone under and squeeze the glute of the kneeling side, then shift forward a little until the front of that hip stretches. Don\'t arch your back. For a pelvis that tips forward.

Lie on your side, bottom knee bent. Top leg straight, toes pointing forward, not up. Lift it a hand\'s height, slightly behind your body, and lower slowly. The side of the hip that keeps knees and feet tracking straight.
Foot flat, sitting or standing. Without curling your toes, draw the ball of your foot toward your heel so the arch lifts. Hold, relax. With feet pointing forward when you walk, against duck feet.
Feet apart, hands on your lower back. Lean back gently from the waist, hips forward, as far as is comfortable, and come back up. The quick undo after sitting.
Get up and walk: to the kitchen, around the room, up the stairs. Stand tall, feet pointing forward.
Stand tall, a hand on something for balance. Rise onto your toes, pause, lower slowly.
Long step stance, back heel up. Tuck your tailbone under and squeeze the back glute until the front of that hip stretches. Stay tall.
On your side, elbow under your shoulder, legs straight and stacked. Lift your hips into one straight line and hold. Hold longer as it gets easy.
Hands under your shoulders, body in one straight line: lower your chest, push back up. Start with your hands on a counter, then a chair, then the floor.
Sit back to a chair with a hip hinge, touch it lightly, stand up through your heels. A lower seat as it gets easy; no deep squats under load yet.
One foot forward, one back, upright. Lower the back knee only as far as feels fine, push back up through the front foot.
A band around a door handle, or a loaded backpack with your free hand on a table and your back flat. Pull your elbow back to your ribs, shoulder blade back, lower slowly.
Like the glute bridge with one foot on the floor and the other knee pulled in. Lift and lower without your hips tipping.
A backpack or light dumbbells held close. Hinge as practiced, back flat, down to just below the knees, up by squeezing your glutes. Add weight only when the next morning is no worse.
Carry one heavy bag in one hand and walk tall without leaning. Switch hands.
Morning check-in, an evening routine, stand-up breaks from the PC

A check-in and press-ups when you wake, a short routine in the evening, stand-up breaks from the PC add-on while you sit. Prompted like the cards, when you\'re on your phone. Off until you pick a program.
For disc-related back or leg pain (sciatica): press-ups, spine-sparing core work, walking, posture work that loads nothing.
Strength three days a week, bodyweight first, with the same core and posture work.
A self-care routine, not a diagnosis or treatment. If things stop improving or get worse, see a physio; a McKenzie-trained one suits back pain like this.
Rehab set, then posture · about 15 min
Bead: evening done. Dot: where the leg pain reached that morning, darker lower.
Extension, spine-sparing core work, walking, and posture work that loads nothing.
Strength every other day at most: bodyweight in weeks 1 and 2, light loads from week 3. The recovery set stays as the warm-up. Week %1$d.

No heavy lifting.
No deep squats or crouching under load.
No bending forward with a rounded lower back under load.
No twisting under load.
No hamstring stretching, sit-ups, crunches or toe touches.
No bending forward in the first hour after waking.
Ready to rebuild when the leg pain stays above the knee, mornings are easy, and nothing has flared for a couple of weeks. Bring things back one at a time.
Start Rebuild? Strength comes in every other day, bodyweight first. You can go back to Recovery any time.
From the PC add-on after 25 minutes of sitting, one at a time, in this order.

Discomfort up to 3–4 out of 10 is fine if it's no worse the next morning.
Pain moving up toward the back is a good sign. Pain moving back down the leg and staying a few days: back off to the rehab set.
Bend with a hip hinge. Break up sitting every 20–30 minutes.
Brace for sneezes and coughs: stand tall, slight arch.
Walk with your feet pointing forward and push off the big toe.
Strength needs fuel: protein at every meal and a little more food than feels normal. Without dairy: eggs, fish, meat, tofu, lentils, pea or soy protein.
Numbness in the groin or inner thighs, changes in bladder or bowel control, foot weakness or foot drop, or symptoms in both legs.
Morning: at the first unlock after a night. Evening: from the time set, while you\'re on your phone. Held back during calls, Do Not Disturb, a Bluetooth pause and a snooze.
The pain has reached the knee or lower three mornings running after being higher: back off to the rehab set only. If it stays there, see a physio.
Worse this morning after yesterday\'s strength session: keep today to the rehab set, and go lighter next time.
First hour after waking: no bending forward. Hinge at the hips; for socks, sit and bring the foot up.
Where does the leg pain reach this morning?
%1$s. Floor space and a few minutes.
Get in position, then tap the orb
A McKenzie extension: arching the lower back gently, which tends to ease pain from a disc pressing on a nerve and pull leg pain back toward the spine.

Lie face down, forehead on your hands, and let your lower back relax for a few breaths.
Place your hands flat under your shoulders, elbows bent.
Push your chest up with your arms only: your hips and legs stay on the floor, your buttocks and back stay soft.
Breathe out at the top, then lower slowly.
Each rep a little higher, as far as is comfortable; with straight arms at the top once it's easy.
A stretch or pressure in the lower back. Leg pain easing or moving up toward the back is what you want.
Lifting the hips off the floor. Tensing the buttocks. Pushing into sharp pain or pain spreading further down the leg: stop and go lower.
One of McGill\'s spine-sparing core exercises: the trunk holds still while an arm and the opposite leg reach, training the muscles that protect the back.

On hands and knees: hands under your shoulders, knees under your hips, back flat, neck long.
Brace gently, as if someone might poke your belly.
Slide one arm forward and the opposite leg back until both are level with your body.
Hold, keeping your hips level and your back still: no sagging, no twisting.
Return slowly and switch sides.
The buttock of the leg that reaches, the muscles along your spine, the shoulder of the arm.
Kicking the leg high and arching the back. Hips tipping to one side. Rushing: slow and still is the point.
McGill\'s side plank, from the knees: trains the deep muscles at the side of the trunk (quadratus lumborum, obliques) without loading the spine.

Lie on your side, elbow under your shoulder, forearm flat in front, knees bent behind you.
Stack your hips and shoulders, top hand on your hip or shoulder.
Lift your hips until your body is straight from knees to head.
Hold, breathing normally.
Lower, then turn over for the other side.
The side of your waist on the bottom side, the shoulder holding you up.
Hips sagging or pushed back. Shoulder shrugged to the ear. Holding your breath.
McGill\'s curl-up: works the front abs while the lower back keeps its natural curve, unlike a sit-up or crunch, which bend the spine.

Lie on your back, one knee bent, the other leg straight.
Slide your hands under the small of your back to keep its curve.
Brace gently. Lift your head and shoulders a little off the floor, as one block, chin slightly tucked.
Hold, breathing.
Lower; switch which knee is bent halfway through.
The front of your belly, working without moving much.
Curling the neck or pulling on your head. Flattening the lower back into your hands. Lifting high: a few centimetres is enough.
Wakes up the glutes, which take the load off the lower back and keep the pelvis from tipping forward.

Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat and hip-width apart, arms by your sides.
Squeeze your glutes first.
Lift your hips until your body is straight from shoulders to knees.
Hold at the top without arching your back.
Lower slowly, one vertebra at a time.
Your buttocks, then the backs of your thighs.
Arching the lower back at the top. Pushing through the toes. Feeling it mostly in the hamstrings: bring your feet a little closer.
The safe way to bend: the hips fold and the back stays straight, so the spine isn\'t rounded under load. The movement to use for socks, the floor and lifting.

Stand tall, feet hip-width apart, knees soft.
Hands on your hip creases, or a broomstick along your back touching head, upper back and tailbone.
Push your hips back as if closing a car door behind you; your chest goes forward.
Go only as far as your back stays straight; the stick stays in contact.
Come up by squeezing your glutes and pushing your hips forward.
A stretch at the backs of the thighs, the glutes working on the way up. Not the lower back.
Bending at the waist instead of the hips. Bending the knees into a squat. Letting the lower back round.
Retrains the deep neck muscles that hold the head over the shoulders, against the forward head posture of phones and screens (the \"neck hump\").

Sit or stand tall, or lie on your back with your head on the floor.
Look straight ahead, chin level.
Glide your head straight back, making a double chin, as if a string pulled the back of your head.
Hold, feeling the back of the neck lengthen.
Relax forward to neutral, not further.
A stretch at the base of the skull, the front of the neck working gently.
Nodding the chin down to the chest. Tilting the head back. Pushing hard: it\'s a small, gentle move.
Wakes the muscles between the shoulder blades that hold the shoulders back, against rounded shoulders.

Stand or sit tall, arms by your sides or elbows bent at your sides.
Draw your shoulder blades back and down, toward your back pockets.
Hold the squeeze, chest open.
Relax slowly.
Between and below your shoulder blades.
Shrugging the shoulders up. Arching the lower back. Pushing the chin forward.
Stretches the chest muscles that pull the shoulders forward after hours at a desk or on a phone.

Stand in a doorway. Forearm on the frame, elbow at shoulder height, upper arm out to the side.
Step one foot through the doorway.
Lean forward gently until the front of your chest stretches.
Hold and breathe; ease further as it lets go.
Switch arms, or do both at once.
Across the front of the chest and shoulder.
Arching the lower back to lean. Tingling down the arm: lower the elbow. Bouncing.
Mobilises the upper back and shoulders and trains the muscles that keep them back.

Stand with your head, upper back and hips against a wall, feet a step out, knees soft.
Arms against the wall in a W: elbows bent, backs of the hands on the wall.
Slide your arms up toward a Y, keeping elbows and hands on the wall.
Go only as high as they stay on the wall.
Slide back down to the W.
The upper back and between the shoulder blades; a stretch at the front of the shoulders.
Arching the lower back off the wall to reach higher. Shrugging. Forcing the range: it grows with time.
Stretches the front of the hip (hip flexors), which tighten from sitting and tip the pelvis forward (anterior pelvic tilt).

Kneel on one knee on a cushion, the other foot flat in front, both knees at about 90°.
Stand tall. Tuck your tailbone under: flatten your lower back slightly.
Squeeze the glute of the kneeling side.
Shift your weight forward a little until the front of that hip stretches.
Hold and breathe, then switch sides.
The front of the hip and top of the thigh of the kneeling leg.
Arching the lower back to go further. Leaning the trunk forward. Letting the front knee cave in.
Strengthens the side of the hip (gluteus medius), which keeps the knees and feet pointing straight when you walk, against duck feet.

Lie on your side, head on your lower arm, bottom knee bent for balance.
Top leg straight, in line with your body or slightly behind it.
Turn the toes forward or slightly down, not up to the ceiling.
Lift the leg a hand's height, slowly.
Lower slowly; finish one side, then the other.
The side of the hip, just below the belt line.
Rolling back and turning the toes up (the wrong muscle takes over). Swinging the leg. Lifting high.
Strengthens the small muscles of the arch, which help the foot and ankle hold their line when you walk.

Sit with your foot flat on the floor, then progress to standing.
Keep your toes long and relaxed.
Draw the ball of your foot toward your heel, so the arch rises, without curling the toes.
Hold, then relax.
Switch feet.
Under the arch of the foot.
Curling or gripping with the toes. Rolling the foot onto its outer edge.
The McKenzie extension standing up: undoes the bent posture of sitting, anywhere, in a few seconds.

Stand with your feet apart.
Place your hands on your lower back, fingers pointing down.
Lean back gently from the waist, letting your hips move forward.
Go as far as is comfortable, then come back up.
Repeat smoothly.
Gentle pressure in the lower back that eases with the reps.
Leaning back from the neck. Bending the knees. Pushing into sharp or spreading leg pain.
A short walk: the easiest way to break up sitting, and walking is one of the best things for a recovering back.

Get up.
Walk for two minutes: to the kitchen, around the room, up the stairs.
Stand tall, feet pointing forward, push off the big toe.
Let your arms swing.
Checking the phone while walking. Shuffling with the feet turned out.
Strengthens the calves and the push-off of the foot, and gets the blood moving after sitting.

Stand tall, feet hip-width apart, a hand on something for balance.
Rise onto the balls of your feet, as high as you can.
Pause at the top.
Lower slowly, over two or three seconds.
Rolling onto the outer edges of the feet. Dropping down fast.
The hip flexor stretch standing up, for the desk: same idea as the kneeling one.

Take a long step forward, back heel up, both feet pointing forward.
Stand tall.
Tuck your tailbone under and squeeze the back glute.
Shift forward a little until the front of the back hip stretches.
Hold, then switch legs.
The front of the hip of the back leg.
Arching the lower back. Leaning forward.
The full side plank, from the feet, once the knee version is easy.

Lie on your side, elbow under your shoulder, legs straight and stacked (or top foot in front).
Brace gently.
Lift your hips into a straight line from feet to head.
Hold, breathing.
Lower and switch sides; hold longer as it gets easy.
The side of the waist, the shoulder.
Hips sagging or piking. Holding your breath.
Upper-body strength (chest, shoulders, arms) with the trunk held straight, a plank that moves.

Hands a little wider than your shoulders, on a counter, a chair, then the floor as it gets easier.
Body in one straight line from head to heels, belly braced.
Lower your chest toward your hands, elbows at about 45° from your body.
Push back up without letting the hips sag.
The chest, the backs of the arms, the front of the shoulders.
Sagging hips or arched back. Elbows flared straight out. Head dropping.
A squat with a target: sitting back to a chair teaches the hip hinge and builds the legs without going deep.

Stand in front of a chair, feet shoulder-width apart.
Push your hips back and bend your knees, chest forward, back straight.
Touch the seat lightly; don't flop down.
Stand up by pushing through your heels and squeezing your glutes.
Use a lower seat as it gets easy.
The front of the thighs and the glutes.
Rounding the lower back at the bottom. Knees caving in. Rocking to get up.
Builds the legs one at a time, with an upright back, which is easier on the spine than a loaded squat.

Take a long step: one foot forward, the back heel up.
Stand tall, hands on your hips.
Lower the back knee toward the floor, both knees bending.
Go only as low as feels fine.
Push up through the front foot; finish one side, then the other.
The front thigh and glute of the front leg.
Leaning forward. The front knee caving in. The front heel lifting.
Strengthens the upper back, the counterpart to all the sitting and screen time.

Loop a band around a door handle, or hold a loaded backpack with your free hand on a table and your back flat.
Arm straight, shoulder down.
Pull your elbow back to your ribs, squeezing the shoulder blade back.
Pause, then lower slowly.
Between the shoulder blades, the back of the shoulder.
Shrugging. Twisting the trunk to pull. Rounding the back with the backpack.
The glute bridge on one leg: more load for the glutes, and it shows if one side is weaker.

Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat.
Lift one foot and hold that knee toward your chest, or keep the leg straight in line.
Push through the heel of the foot on the floor and lift your hips.
Keep the hips level at the top.
Lower slowly; finish one side, then the other.
The buttock of the working leg.
Hips tipping to one side. Arching the back. Cramping hamstring: bring the foot closer.
The hip hinge with a weight (a Romanian deadlift), once the bodyweight hinge is easy: strength for the back of the legs and the glutes, with a straight back.

Stand holding a backpack or light dumbbells in front of your thighs.
Knees soft, back straight, shoulders back.
Push your hips back and slide the weight down your thighs, close to your legs.
Stop just below the knees, or before your back starts to round.
Come up by squeezing your glutes.
The backs of the thighs and the glutes.
Rounding the lower back. The weight drifting away from the legs. Going heavy too soon: only add weight when the next morning is no worse.
Carrying a weight on one side: the trunk muscles work hard to keep you upright, a real-life strength for the back.

Pick up a heavy bag in one hand, using a hip hinge.
Stand tall, shoulders level.
Walk 30 to 40 metres without leaning or swinging.
Put it down with a hinge and switch hands.
The side of the waist opposite the bag, the grip, the shoulders.
Leaning away from the bag. Shrugging the carrying shoulder.
